Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (basis for Year Established -62): Cicero, Pro Flacco 28.68, on the Temple contributions ('aurum Iudaeorum') seized by L. Valerius Flaccus, proconsul of Asia 62/61 BCE: c. 100 pounds of gold at Apamea, a little over 20 pounds at Laodicea, [100?] at Adramyttium, 'Pergami non multum' (not much at Pergamum). Funds collected for Jerusalem at Pergamum imply resident Jews, apparently a small community. No count: Population blank. Earlier contacts that are not resident presence and so are not rows: the Pergamene decree in favour of the Jews quoted by Josephus, Ant. 14.247-255 (Roman senatus consultum brought to Pergamum, envoys of the high priest Hyrcanus, the claim that the Pergamenes' ancestors were friends of the Jews 'in the days of Abraham'), dated by most to John Hyrcanus I (c. 113-112 BCE, or c. 130 BCE by others); and the Roman letter of 139 BCE commending the Jews to King Attalus (1 Macc 15:22). A tourist guide (jguideeurope) claims Jews lived in the city from the 2nd c. BCE but gives no source.

Encyclopaedia Judaica (I. Gafni), 'Pergamum': 'By the first century B.C.E. a Jewish community existed in Pergamum, as Cicero refers to the confiscation of funds in Pergamum intended for the Temple in Jerusalem (Pro Flacco 28:68).' Scholarly assessment of the same Flaccus evidence (62/61 BCE); organized community, size not given. The article also cites the Pergamene decree (Ant. 14.247-55, probably c. 113-112 BCE under John Hyrcanus I) and Herod's gifts to Pergamum (War 1.425, Herodian period), which are diplomatic/benefaction contacts rather than evidence of resident Jews.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Flaccus, L. Valerius': Flaccus (proconsul of Asia 62-61 BCE, tried 59 BCE) seized Temple money in several cities, 'at Pergamon, a small sum, as probably not many Jews were living there at that time.' Same Cicero evidence as the other rows; suggests a small Jewish community. Note: the Jewish Encyclopedia article 'Pergamus (Bergama)' states 'there are no documents to show that Jews lived there in ancient times' (disagreeing; it ignores Cicero). The regional figure of 180,000 Jews in Asia Minor (T. Reinach, from the Flaccus sums; 'possibly ten times too large' per JE 'Asia Minor') is regional and not Pergamon's population.
